source_text: Ingerit quippe omnibus scripturis suis, Adam atque Evam bonos tantum a Deo conditos, id est, nulli naturali crimini mancipatos, eosque libera voluntate peccasse, sed ita granditer, ut omnia in natura sua Dei instituta subruerent. Illud enim, inquit, peccatum valde maius atque altius diabolus infixit, quam sunt ista hominibus nota peccata. Unde illo magno primi hominis peccato, natura ibi nostra, in deterius commutata, non solum facta est peccatrix, verum etiam generat peccatores; et tamen ipse languor, quo bene vivendi virtus periit, non est natura, sed vitium. Illud ergo peccatum, quod ipsum hominem in paradiso mutavit in peius, quia multo est grandius quam iudicare nos possumus [n10] , ab omni nascente trahitur. Ecce quam aperte quid sentiret exposuit: Primi, inquit, illi homines bonam habuere naturam, sed peccatum tam immane, tam inaestimabile perpetrarunt, ut virtutem bene vivendi interimerent, liberi arbitrii lumen exstinguerent, facerent in reliquum peccandi necessitatem; ne cui esset possibile de eorum stirpe nascenti, in virtutum decora conari, et declinatis vitiis compotem fieri sanctitatis.
pass_a_gloss: For he pours into all his writings that Adam and Eve were founded by God only good, that is enslaved to no natural charge, and that they sinned by a free will, but so greatly that they undermined all God's institutions in their nature. For that sin, he says, the devil fixed far greater and deeper than those sins known to humans. Whence by that great sin of the first human, our nature there, changed into the worse, was not only made a sinner, but even generates sinners; and nevertheless that languor itself, by which the virtue of living well perished, is not nature but vice. That sin therefore, which changed the human himself in paradise into the worse, because it is much greater than we can judge, is drawn from every one being born. Behold how openly he set out what he sensed: Those first humans, he says, had a good nature, but they perpetrated a sin so huge, so inestimable, that they killed the virtue of living well, extinguished the light of free decision, made for the rest a necessity of sinning; lest it be possible for anyone being born from their stock to try toward the becoming things of virtues, and, vices having been declined, to become possessor of holiness.

lemmas.lexica: LS necessitas; Blaise vs free choice
LS naturalis; Blaise malum naturale=evil as a nature
LS voluntas=will, wish; Blaise moral will
LS arbitrium=judgment, free decision; Blaise liberum arbitrium
LS liber=free; Blaise unde liberum est abstinere
LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself

pass_b_english: He presses into all his writings the claim that only Adam and Eve were made good by God—that is, subject to no natural guilt—and that they sinned by free will, but so greatly that they overthrew everything God had established in their nature. He says: ‘The devil planted that sin far greater and deeper than the sins familiar to people. Therefore, through that great sin of the first human, our nature was changed for the worse there, and not only became sinful but also generates sinners. Yet the very sickness through which the power of living well perished is not nature but a defect. That sin which changed the human being for the worse in paradise, because it is far greater than we can judge, is inherited by everyone born’ (compare Augustine, Marriage and Sexual Desire 2.34.57–58).

See how openly he explained his meaning! Those first humans, he says, had a good nature, but committed a sin so monstrous and immeasurable that they destroyed the power to live well, extinguished the light of free will, and established a necessity of sinning thereafter. No one born from their stock could strive toward the beauty of virtues, turn away from vices, and attain holiness.

choices.why: Glossary default: arbitrium is the decision-power, not a later Augustinian/Reformation free-will locus.
Julian's definition of sin is an act of will. Keep 'will' rather than later 'free will' system language unless liberum arbitrium is present.
Freedom to abstain is required for will and sin.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
